newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan to work together on deregulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan to work together on deregulation.

text.p: The United States and Japan have agreed to work together as Tokyo deregulates the Japanese economy and as Washington tries to increase access to the Japanese market for foreign businesses.

U.S. officials hailed the pact, reached early on Thursday, as a way to reduce Washington's huge trade deficit with Tokyo, but Japanese officials flatly rejected the idea that the United States would have any supervisory role in their economy.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the agreement would allow U.S. officials to have input in Japan's deregulation though "bilateral consultations" on such areas as telecommunications, financial services and medical equipment.
Officials said the agreement was designed to increase U.S. market access to Japan, which would reduce the two countries' growing trade imbalance.
"They recognise that the trade imbalance works to their long-term detriment," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters.
She said this would be the first time the United States would have such a role in seeking to affect Japanese policy.
But Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said explicitly that the United States would not have an advisory or supervisory role on Japan's efforts to deregulate key sectors of its economy.
"It's not an advisory role," Hashimoto said, speaking through an interpreter. "We have no intention of being supervised. Deregulation is a task that we have to embark upon for ourselves."

Clinton, who arrived in Denver on Thursday for a weekend summit with leaders of the Group of Seven industrialised countries and Russia, said he wished the U.S. trade deficit with Japan was not so high.
He said he would discuss the issue during his meeting with Hashimoto on Thursday afternoon.
Earlier on Thursday, the U.S. Commerce Department said that the U.S. deficit with Japan grew by 5.1 percent to $4.84 billion in April.
On Wednesday, Japan said that its merchandise trade surplus with the United States surged 93 percent in May from a year earlier to 322.87 billion yen ($2.85 billion).
Barshefsky described the agreement as "very exciting" and said the potential trade in the sectors involved was "very substantial."
